alt: A vector is split into two rotated components. The two vertical contributions stack to form the sine of the total angle.
The first rotated component moves right; the second moves left. Their signed horizontal displacements give cosine of the sum.
Rotating the upward vector counterclockwise moves its tip left. Its horizontal component is minus sine b.
Points at b and minus b reflect across the horizontal axis: cosine stays the same and sine changes sign.
Two successive rotations by x produce a total rotation of two x.
Graph of sine with its tangent at zero. The tangent rises one unit for each unit to the right, matching cosine zero equals one.
Graph of cosine with tangent slope minus one at pi over two; cosine crosses zero while decreasing.
The inner triangle lies inside the unit circle sector, which lies inside the triangle formed by the tangent at one zero. Their areas squeeze sine h over h.
Two points on sine define a secant. A right triangle marks horizontal change h and vertical change delta y; their ratio approaches the tangent slope.
Four derivative arrows form a cycle: sine, cosine, negative sine, negative cosine, then sine again.
A chain differentiates x squared four times: two x, two, zero, zero. It shows the superscript four counting operations.
Two linked changes: x to three x, with rate three, then the angle to its sine, with rate cosine. The rates multiply.
Two columns show all four derivatives. The final highlighted row contains sine x and minus six x to the minus four.
The coefficient and exponent follow separate branches: minus one times minus two gives two, while minus two minus one gives minus three.
The first logarithm derivative produces x to the minus one. Each further step adds the next negative integer factor, explaining the factorial and alternating signs.
Only the part of X outside Y is shaded. The overlap and the right-only part are unshaded.
X contains one and three in its left-only region and two in the overlap. Y contains four in its right-only region. Only one and three are shaded.
The same sets are shown, but only the right-only region of Y, containing four, is shaded.
All three sample elements in X are crossed out when X is removed from itself. The output is the empty set.
A radius from the centre h k to a point x y forms a right triangle with horizontal distance x minus h and vertical distance y minus k.
The ellipse has horizontal intercepts minus two and two, vertical intercepts minus one and one, and dimension arrows marking full width four and height two.
A tall ellipse has horizontal intercepts plus and minus three and vertical intercepts plus and minus five. Dimension arrows show six across and ten vertically.
The four axis intercepts of a general ellipse are labelled minus a zero, a zero, zero b, and zero minus b.
A shifted circle is centred at three minus two. A horizontal radius of four reaches seven minus two. Dashed projections locate the centre.
A circle diameter is split at the centre into two equal radii. An arrow leads to circumference equals pi times diameter.
A circle is cut into twelve sectors. Alternating upward and downward sectors form a strip with curved edges; in the limit its base tends to pi r and its height to r.
A unit circle on a square grid is stretched into an ellipse on a rectangular grid. A highlighted grid cell shows horizontal and vertical scale factors multiplying area.
An upward parabola has focus above the origin and a horizontal directrix below it. A point on the curve has two equal marked distances: to the focus and straight down to the directrix.
The two hyperbola branches open left and right from vertices plus and minus a. Diagonals through a rectangle of half-width a and half-height b show the asymptote slopes.
Three standard conics are compared: a closed ellipse from a sum of squares, a two-branch hyperbola from a difference of squares, and a parabola from one squared and one linear coordinate.
Eighteen dots form six complete boxes of three, with no leftover dot. This witnesses three divides eighteen.
Multiples of a appear at equally spaced marked positions on a number line, illustrating that an integer number of steps of size a reaches a divisible number. The sketch assumes positive a.
On a number line, three lies only one sixth of the way from zero to eighteen. It cannot be reached by an integer number of eighteen-unit steps.
Six boxes contain three dots each, accounting for eighteen dots. A separate highlighted nineteenth dot remains outside the boxes.
Two branches distinguish notation: three divides eighteen evaluates to true, while the fraction three over eighteen evaluates to one sixth.
The true divisibility claim and false claim that eleven is not prime feed an OR operation, whose output is true.
A four-row truth table for inclusive OR highlights the false-false row, the only row whose result is false.
Two product rows align positive and negative mixed terms. Highlighted pairs cancel, leaving a cubed minus b cubed.
Aligned product rows for the sum of cubes cancel the opposite mixed terms and leave positive endpoint cubes.
Rows labelled multiplication by a and by negative b show all six products. Opposite mixed terms cancel in matched columns.
A substitution diagram changes b to negative b in the difference identity, then simplifies to the sum-of-cubes factors.
A vertical substitution diagram rewrites twenty-seven as three cubed, inserts x and three into the identity, and simplifies the quadratic terms.
The bases two x and five are substituted into the sum-of-cubes identity. Each squared and mixed term is evaluated explicitly.
The factorised fraction marks the same product in numerator and denominator. The result retains the exclusions x not equal to plus or minus three.
The graph is a horizontal line at height one with an open circle at x equals three. The missing point shows the domain restriction survives cancellation.
Two separate unit cubes have total volume two. Beside them, a cube of side two is divided by three midplanes into eight unit cubes, showing the extra volume when the sum is cubed.
